Senses.Explanation: Literally, a 'source-line teacher' or 'lineage master': the ancestral source-line (宗) joined to teacher (師). The term occurs 1,445 times in 257 allowed texts and names a teacher judged or presented in relation to the Chan lineage. A collected assembly address gives a direct role statement: 'As for a lineage master, he takes away the poor child's pearl sewn in his clothes and examines the accomplished person's viewpoint' (夫宗師者，奪貧子之衣珠，究達人之見處). Dahui says, 'In general a lineage master decides right and wrong and must open people's eyes; he cannot rely only on blind cangues and sightless blows' (大凡宗師決斷是非。要得開人眼目。不可一向盲枷瞎棒). Yuanwu calls Zhaozhou 'a great-handed lineage master' (大手宗師) and records that he does not discuss mystery, marvel, occasion, or object but meets people solely with the fundamental matter. Yuanwu also calls Dongshan Shouchu, Zhimen Guangzuo, Deshan Yuanmi, and Xianglin Chengyuan 'great lineage masters' (皆為大宗師). The label can be withheld or mocked: a case anthology says of an inadequate answer, 'calling oneself a lineage master like this and wanting to open the eyes of humans and gods—only in the donkey year' (如此自稱宗師，欲開人天眼目，驢年去). The records therefore use the noun as title, appraisal, role description, and rebuke of a failed claimant.
Senses.Note: All direct-definition formulas and common modifiers were searched. 'Great lineage master' (大宗師) occurs 113 times in 49 texts; 'lineage-master household' (宗師家) occurs 87 times in 47; 'lineage-master eye' (宗師眼) occurs 22 times in 20; and 'a generation's lineage master' (一代宗師) occurs nine times in eight. The role is corpus-wide and is not keyed to a single teacher.

Senses.Explanation: The governing or essential purport of a teaching, transmission, house, or master. The corpus records two overlapping deployments. First, the purport is transmitted or fixed. In the Bodhidharma narrative, the seal of the teaching is transmitted to tally with verified mind, while the robe is conferred outwardly to fix the purport. A later preface parallels Shakyamuni holding up the flower and transmitting the subtle mind to Kashyapa with Bodhidharma facing the wall and entrusting the purport to Shenguang, later named Huike. Other formulas speak of revealing the purport and receiving it personally. Second, the purport belongs to a named house or teacher. A biography says someone awakened to Huanglong's purport. Another exchange calls raising the teaching banner and establishing the purport the teacher's ordinary tea and rice. Dedicatory prose says a compiler gathered the material to completion and thereby fixed the purport. The noun takes verbs translated as fix, establish, clarify, receive, reveal, and bury; named forms include Bodhidharma's purport and the purport of the buddha teaching. The records give the governing object and verb each time rather than a separate universal definition.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense covering transmitted purport and the purport of a named house. Current count: 2,171 matches in 315 files; 'clarify the purport' 99/71; 'this purport' 10/4; 'Bodhidharma's purport' 2/2; 'the purport of the buddha teaching' 3/3. The selected occurrences are transmission narrative, preface, biography, stock question, and dedicatory prose, so their occurrence master keys remain null. The formula ending in 'as for the purport' refers to people who take something as their purport and does not define the noun.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the 'source-gate' or 'lineage gate.' The term occurs 1,934 times in 285 allowed texts. Yuanwu supplies a direct graph relation: 'Buddha's words take mind as the source; when the source is penetrated, speech is also penetrated; since it is called the source-gate...' (佛語心為宗。宗通說亦通。既謂之宗門). Across encounter records, the compound names the Chan lineage as the field within which a matter, question, or saying is presented. 'Within the lineage gate' (宗門中) occurs 350 times in 108 texts, and 'under the lineage gate' (宗門下) occurs 175 times in 71 texts. A lecturer explicitly sets aside the three vehicles and twelve divisions of teaching and asks, 'What is the matter within the lineage gate?' (三乘十二分教即不問如何是宗門中事). Another monk asks the teacher to raise and proclaim 'the matter within the lineage gate' (宗門中事。請師舉唱). Fachang Yiyu draws a line with his staff, sets that aside, and asks how the lineage-gate matter goes (這箇即且止，宗門事作麼生). Wuyi Yuanlai contrasts what he calls the utmost reach of the teaching families with 'the strong point within the lineage gate' (宗門中長處), and elsewhere asks directly what that strong point is. The same word also heads titles of collected lineage records; those titles attest the institutional and textual range without creating a separate sense.
Senses.Note: Definition-formula searches found Yuanwu's explicit derivation and three occurrences of 'called the lineage gate.' Sixty-three occurrences in 31 texts ask 'what is the lineage gate' or a longer question beginning that way. The corpus-wide sense covers lineage, its recorded affairs, and collection titles; no master-specific meaning was established. The English target does not leave the graph meaning to a religious loanword.

Senses.Explanation: The two graphs mean “lineage or house” and “wind”: “the wind of a house,” its characteristic manner or style. A preface names “the Caodong house wind” and describes it as the wondrous accord of upright and inclined. The expression takes verbs meaning expand, rouse, inherit, and revive: one may greatly expand a house wind, vigorously rouse it, inherit it later, or revive the Caodong house wind. Biographical language places inheriting the house wind beside fulfilling a Guiyang prediction, greatly rousing the ancestral working, and transmitting the true eye of the teaching. The house wind can itself become the object of a question: “What is the phrase by which the house wind does not fall?” Related expressions are “family wind,” “gate wind,” and “essential purport.” The records use the term for a lineage's manner without reducing it to one fixed list of traits.
Senses.Note: This is one corpus-wide sense. It may attach to a named house and combines with verbs of expansion, rousing, inheritance, and revival. The curated passages are prefaces, biographical narrative, and a multi-speaker question, so their speaker fields remain null. Compare “family wind,” “gate wind,” and “essential purport.”
